title: I was a truck driver when a woman climbed out of a coffin at a rest stop — then she begged me to drive away before the funeral director returned (PART 2)

blocks.text: …move the others before anyone can find them."
She nodded hard. "They cross us out when they take us. Not when we die. Nobody's supposed to die. They just want our money."

The man came out of the restroom just as the first state trooper pulled into the lot. He saw the open van doors, saw my truck, and walked very fast toward the driver's side. The trooper got there first. The funeral director, who wasn't one, was in handcuffs before he got his keys out.

Her name was Teresa Vance. She was fifty-six, a recently widowed retired schoolteacher from Iowa. Six months earlier, she'd started attending a free "grief and wellness" program at a private clinic in Des Moines. So had the five other women in the photograph. All of them were widows.
All of them had inherited money or property.

The clinic's director, a charming man who called himself a doctor and wasn't, used the sessions to gain their trust. Then he had them sign documents they thought were consent forms for a wellness retreat. They were really powers of attorney and property transfers. When a woman's paperwork was complete, she was sedated during a "treatment," reported to her distant relatives as having died suddenly, and moved in a funeral van, which no one ever stops or searches, to a remote ranch in western Nebraska. There she was kept sedated and isolated while the director emptied her accounts and sold her house.
The unmarked coffin was for the sixth woman in the photo, Gloria. The appointment for her "treatment" was the following Monday.
Teresa had woken up early because her body processed the sedative faster than they'd expected.
She'd kicked the coffin lid loose with both feet.
The troopers called in the Nebraska State Patrol and the FBI. That afternoon, I sat in my cab with a cup of terrible gas station coffee and watched a convoy of SUVs heading west.

They found the ranch eighty miles away. All five women were there, alive, in locked bedrooms, groggy and weak. One had been there nearly four months. Her family had already held a memorial service. Two staff members were arrested at the ranch; the clinic director was arrested in Des Moines that evening, and Gloria was contacted before her appointment.

The case took more than a year to prosecute. Investigators recovered most of the money. Three of the women got their houses back. A doctor who had signed false death certificates lost his license and went to prison along with the director.
Teresa calls me every year on the anniversary.
The first year, she and the five other women sent me a card signed by all of them. Gloria signed it too, with a note: "You never met me, but I owe you my life."
I've been driving for twenty-three years. I've stopped at a thousand rest areas. Now I always look twice at the vans parked beside me.
